tips.title: One rule picks both acids
tips.body: **The acid must not add the ion being tested for.** Halide test → **not hydrochloric** (supplies chloride). Sulfate test → **not sulfuric** (supplies sulfate). Learn the rule and you can never swap them.

tips.title: Burning for hydrogen, glowing for oxygen
tips.body: Hydrogen: a **burning** splint, and the gas **pops**. Oxygen: a **glowing** splint, and it **relights**. Match the state of the splint to the gas, and give the result as well as the method.

tips.title: Excess sodium hydroxide finds only aluminium
tips.body: Aluminium, calcium and magnesium all give **white**. Only **aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess** — so that test identifies aluminium and leaves the other two undistinguished. A **flame test** separates those.

tips.title: The carbonate test has two stages
tips.body: Fizzing shows **a gas**; only **limewater turning milky** shows it was **carbon dioxide**. An answer that stops at the fizzing has done half the test.

tips.title: Two ions, two tests
tips.body: An ionic compound has a **cation** and an **anion**. Flame test or sodium hydroxide for the metal; silver nitrate, barium chloride or acid for the non-metal. A question giving two results wants **both halves** named.

steps.title: The four gas tests
steps.body:
Four gases, four tests, and each has a **method** and a **result**. A question wants both.

**Hydrogen.** Hold a **burning splint** at the **open end** of a test tube of the gas. The hydrogen **burns rapidly with a pop**.

**Oxygen.** Insert a **glowing splint** into a test tube of the gas. The splint **relights**.

**Carbon dioxide.** Bubble the gas through, or shake it with, **limewater** — an aqueous solution of **calcium hydroxide**. The limewater **turns milky**, or cloudy.

**Chlorine.** Hold **damp litmus paper** in the gas. The paper is **bleached** and **turns white**.

**The two splint tests are easily confused, and the difference is exact:**

- **hydrogen** needs a **burning** splint, and the gas itself burns with a **pop**
- **oxygen** needs a **glowing** splint, and the splint **relights**

Saying *a lighted splint relights* describes neither test. Match the state of the splint to the gas.

**Two details worth having:**

- **Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution.** If a question calls it that, it is the same thing.
- **The litmus must be damp.** Dry litmus paper is not bleached — the chlorine has to dissolve in the water on the paper first.

steps.title: Flame tests
steps.body:
**Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions — cations.** Five compounds produce distinctive colours:

- **lithium** compounds give a **crimson** flame
- **sodium** compounds give a **yellow** flame
- **potassium** compounds give a **lilac** flame
- **calcium** compounds give an **orange-red** flame
- **copper** compounds give a **green** flame

**The method.** Dip a clean wire loop in the sample and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame. The loop must be **clean** — usually dipped in hydrochloric acid and heated until it gives no colour — because any residue from a previous test would show its own colour.

**The limitation the spec states explicitly:**

> **If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked.**

This matters because it is the **reason instrumental methods exist**. Sodium's yellow is intense, and a trace of sodium can hide the colour of another ion entirely. So a flame test is a good quick test on a **single** compound and unreliable on a **mixture** — which is exactly the weakness the next topic's instruments overcome.

**In an answer**, say **which** colour goes with **which** metal, and if asked for a limitation, give the masking rather than something vague about the test being difficult.

steps.title: Metal hydroxide tests
steps.body:
**Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions.** Adding it to a solution of the unknown produces a **precipitate** whose colour identifies the metal.

**The coloured precipitates are unambiguous:**

- **copper(II)** → **blue**
- **iron(II)** → **green**
- **iron(III)** → **brown**

Those are the same three colours as the transition metal compounds, which is not a coincidence — it is the same chemistry seen from another direction.

**The white precipitates are the problem.** **Aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all form white precipitates**, so the colour alone cannot tell you which you have.

**The solution is to add more sodium hydroxide.**

> **Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.**

So:

- white precipitate that **dissolves in excess** → **aluminium**
- white precipitate that **does not dissolve** → **calcium or magnesium**

**Notice what that test does and does not achieve.** It identifies **aluminium** definitely, and leaves calcium and magnesium **still undistinguished** by this test — for those you would use a **flame test**, since calcium gives orange-red and magnesium gives no colour.

**Being precise about that is a Higher-tier move.** A question asking whether the tests identify the compound has a real answer: aluminium yes, calcium and magnesium only in combination with another test.

steps.title: Carbonates, halides and sulfates
steps.body:
**Carbonates.** **Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas**, which is then **identified with limewater**. So this test has two stages: add acid, then test the gas given off. Fizzing alone is not proof — the limewater turning milky is.

**Halides.** **Halide ions in solution produce precipitates with silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid.**

- **silver chloride** is **white**
- **silver bromide** is **cream**
- **silver iodide** is **yellow**

The three colours run from white through cream to yellow, deepening down the group.

**Sulfates.** **Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.**

**Now notice the two acids**, because this is the most elegant thing in the topic:

| Test | Reagent | Acid added |
|---|---|---|
| halide | silver nitrate | **nitric** acid |
| sulfate | barium chloride | **hydrochloric** acid |

**Why are they different?** Because **the acid must not add the ion you are testing for.**

- Testing for a **halide**, you cannot add **hydrochloric** acid — it would supply **chloride** ions and give a white precipitate whatever the sample contained.
- Testing for a **sulfate**, you cannot add **sulfuric** acid — it would supply **sulfate** ions and give a white precipitate regardless.

So each test uses the acid that **does not contain its own target ion**. One rule picks both acids, and a question asking why a particular acid is used is asking for exactly this.

**What the acid is for.** It removes carbonate ions, which would otherwise produce their own precipitate and give a false positive. So the acid is doing a job, and choosing the wrong one would undo it.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The acid rule is one idea, not two facts.** **The acid must not add the ion being tested for.** Halide test → not hydrochloric, because it supplies chloride. Sulfate test → not sulfuric, because it supplies sulfate. Learn the rule and both acids follow; learn the acids and you will eventually swap them.

**And the acid is not decorative.** It removes **carbonate** ions, which would otherwise form their own precipitate and give a **false positive**. So the test would fail without an acid, and fail differently with the wrong one.

**Burning splint for hydrogen, glowing splint for oxygen.** The pair is confused constantly. Match the **state of the splint** to the gas, and give the **result** as well as the method: hydrogen **pops**, the oxygen splint **relights**.

**Three white precipitates, and the excess test resolves only one.** Aluminium, calcium and magnesium all give white with sodium hydroxide, and **only aluminium dissolves in excess**. So the excess test identifies **aluminium** and leaves **calcium and magnesium** undistinguished — you would need a **flame test**, where calcium gives orange-red and magnesium gives nothing. Saying precisely what a test does *and does not* settle is what separates a careful answer.

**Masking is the stated limitation of flame tests**, and it is the reason the next topic exists. Sodium's yellow is intense enough to hide other colours, so a flame test is reliable on a **single compound** and unreliable on a **mixture**. Quote the masking rather than saying the test is imprecise.

**Damp litmus, not dry.** The chlorine has to dissolve in the water on the paper before it can bleach it. A small word carrying a whole mark.

**The carbonate test has two stages.** Fizzing shows a **gas**; only **limewater turning milky** shows it was **carbon dioxide**. An answer that stops at the fizzing has done half the test.

**Identifying a compound needs two tests.** An ionic compound has a **cation** and an **anion**, so a full identification needs one test for each: a **flame test** or **sodium hydroxide** for the metal, and a **silver nitrate**, **barium chloride** or **acid** test for the non-metal ion. A question giving two results is expecting you to name **both** halves of the compound.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Hydrogen**: a **burning splint** at the open end — it **burns rapidly with a pop**.
- **Oxygen**: a **glowing splint** inserted — it **relights**.
- **Carbon dioxide**: bubbled through **limewater** (calcium hydroxide solution) — it **turns milky**.
- **Chlorine**: **damp** litmus paper — it is **bleached** and turns **white**.
- **Flame tests**: lithium **crimson**, sodium **yellow**, potassium **lilac**, calcium **orange-red**, copper **green**.
- **In a mixture, some flame colours can be masked** — the stated limitation.
- **Sodium hydroxide precipitates**: copper(II) **blue**, iron(II) **green**, iron(III) **brown**.
- **Aluminium, calcium and magnesium** all give **white** precipitates.
- **Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess** sodium hydroxide — so that test identifies **aluminium** and leaves calcium and magnesium undistinguished.
- **Carbonates** react with **dilute acid** to give **carbon dioxide**, identified with **limewater**. Two stages.
- **Halides**: **silver nitrate** with dilute **nitric** acid — chloride **white**, bromide **cream**, iodide **yellow**.
- **Sulfates**: **barium chloride** with dilute **hydrochloric** acid — a **white** precipitate.
- **The acid must not add the ion being tested for** — which is why the two tests use different acids.
- The acid also removes **carbonate** ions, which would give a **false positive**.
- Identifying a compound needs **two** tests: one for the **cation** and one for the **anion**.
- This is **required practical 7**, and section 4.8.3 is **chemistry only**.

questions.prompt: An unknown white solid dissolves in water. Describe the tests you would carry out to identify both ions in the compound, and explain the choice of acid in each test.
questions.solution: Because an ionic compound contains both a positive metal ion and a negative non-metal ion, two separate tests are needed, one for each. To identify the metal ion, a flame test can be carried out by dipping a clean wire loop into the sample and holding it in a blue Bunsen flame. A crimson flame indicates lithium, yellow indicates sodium, lilac indicates potassium, orange red indicates calcium and green indicates copper. The loop must be clean, since residue from a previous test would show its own colour. Alternatively sodium hydroxide solution can be added to a solution of the compound, which gives a blue precipitate for copper two ions, green for iron two and brown for iron three. Aluminium, calcium and magnesium all give white precipitates, and these can be partly distinguished by adding excess sodium hydroxide, since only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves. To identify the negative ion, adding dilute acid and testing the gas with limewater identifies a carbonate if the limewater turns milky. Adding silver nitrate solution in the presence of dilute nitric acid identifies halides, giving a white precipitate for chloride, cream for bromide and yellow for iodide. Adding barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid identifies a sulfate by a white precipitate. The acids differ because the acid must never introduce the ion being tested for. Hydrochloric acid cannot be used in the halide test because it would supply chloride ions and give a false positive, and sulfuric acid cannot be used in the sulfate test because it would supply sulfate ions. The acid is present to remove carbonate ions, which would otherwise form their own precipitate.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Two tests, because an ionic compound has two ions.**

**For the metal ion (cation):**

- **Flame test** — clean wire loop, blue Bunsen flame. **Lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green.** The loop must be **clean**, or residue shows its own colour.
- Or **sodium hydroxide solution** — **copper(II) blue, iron(II) green, iron(III) brown**. **Aluminium, calcium and magnesium all give white**, and adding **excess** distinguishes **aluminium**, which alone **dissolves**.

**For the non-metal ion (anion):**

- **Carbonate** — dilute acid, then **limewater** on the gas: turns **milky**.
- **Halide** — **silver nitrate** with dilute **nitric** acid: chloride **white**, bromide **cream**, iodide **yellow**.
- **Sulfate** — **barium chloride** with dilute **hydrochloric** acid: **white** precipitate.

**Why the acids differ — one rule, applied twice.** **The acid must not add the ion being tested for.**

- Halide test: **not hydrochloric**, which supplies **chloride**.
- Sulfate test: **not sulfuric**, which supplies **sulfate**.

**And what the acid is for:** removing **carbonate** ions, which would otherwise form their own precipitate and give a **false positive**.

questions.prompt: Explain the limitations of the chemical tests in this topic, using flame tests and the white precipitates as your examples.
questions.solution: The chemical tests in this topic are quick and cheap but they have real limitations. The first is that flame tests can be masked. The specification states that if a sample containing a mixture of ions is used, some flame colours can be masked, and sodium in particular produces an intense yellow flame that can conceal the colour of another ion entirely. This means a flame test is reliable on a single pure compound but not on a mixture, and a negative or unexpected result on a mixture cannot be trusted. The second limitation is that some tests do not identify a single ion. When sodium hydroxide solution is added, aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all produce white precipitates, so the colour alone is not enough to identify the metal. Adding excess sodium hydroxide helps only partly, because only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves, so this identifies aluminium but leaves calcium and magnesium still undistinguished from one another. A further test, such as a flame test in which calcium gives an orange red colour and magnesium gives none, would be needed to separate them. A third limitation is that a single test can only identify one ion, so at least two tests are needed to identify an ionic compound fully. These limitations together explain why instrumental methods are valuable, since they are accurate, sensitive and rapid, and can analyse mixtures without the interference that masks a flame test.

examTechnique.body:
Give both the method and the positive result for every test.

Match a burning splint to hydrogen and a glowing splint to oxygen.

Say that the litmus paper must be damp in the chlorine test.

Complete the carbonate test by showing the gas turns limewater milky.

Use nitric acid for halides and hydrochloric acid for sulfates, and explain the choice by saying the acid must not add the ion being tested for.

Remember that excess sodium hydroxide identifies aluminium only.

Use two tests to identify an ionic compound, one for each ion.

Give masking as the limitation of flame tests on a mixture.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the choice of acid as one rule rather than two facts, and can say what the acid is there for. It gives both the method and the result for every test, and it is precise about what a test settles: excess sodium hydroxide identifies aluminium and leaves calcium and magnesium open, which then need a flame test. It quotes masking as the stated limitation of flame tests and sees why that is the reason instrumental methods exist. And it never tries to identify an ionic compound from a single result, because a compound has two ions.
